clue.text: Surrender in some deep-sea raid, perhaps

parts.note: a submarine, a sub, is the deep-sea vessel
a raid is one example of a military mission

explanation.surface: A daring undersea attack ends in capitulation.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text had 'deep-sca', a misreading of 'deep-sea'. A deep-sea raid would be a sub mission; run together the two words make the surrender.
explanation.definitionFit: Yielding to another's authority is an act of submission, so it is a synonym of surrender.

clue.text: Cricketer might produce leg-break?

explanation.surface: A fielder might bowl a spinning delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leg-break' looks like a cricket delivery, but it is a broken leg caused by a fall; in cricket a slip is a fielder beside the wicketkeeper.
explanation.definitionFit: A close fielder in cricket bears this position's name; a stumble or slide on ice can cause a fractured leg.

clue.text: Old Cumberland tradesman?

parts.note: the Duke of Cumberland, victor at Culloden in 1746, earned a gruesome nickname from a meat trade

explanation.surface: A merchant from the old county of Cumberland.
explanation.walkthrough: Cumberland looks like the former English county, famous for its sausage, but it is the Duke of Cumberland, nicknamed for his brutality after Culloden.
explanation.definitionFit: A meat trader is a tradesman, and the Duke's nickname for his bloody suppression of the Jacobites was the same word.

clue.text: Politician whose views were anti-union

parts.note: union suggests trade unions, but it means alliance between nations; opposing such ties is a policy of keeping apart

explanation.surface: A politician who opposed trade unions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anti-union' suggests a foe of trade unions, but the union is any alliance with other countries.
explanation.definitionFit: One favouring a policy of national separation, avoiding foreign alliances, opposes union with others.

clue.text: Likely to learn boss has evidence of debts

parts.note: a boss is a stud, a raised ornament
IOUs are written acknowledgements of debts

explanation.surface: An employer with proof of debts is probably going to learn a lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boss' looks like an employer, but it is a knob or stud on a shield.
explanation.definitionFit: A diligent scholar given to reading is studious, keen and likely to learn.

clue.text: Not too spirited as an opera character?

explanation.surface: Someone a little lacking in liveliness as a role in opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as ONE GIN: one drink only is not too much spirit. Eugene Onegin is the hero of Tchaikovsky's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Just a single measure of spirit is restrained drinking; Tchaikovsky's opera takes its title from Pushkin's hero.

clue.text: Sailor seen on board?

explanation.surface: A seaman spotted on the deck of a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' suggests a ship's deck, but it is a chessboard, where checkmate is announced.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's officer below the captain is a mate; on a chessboard, mate ends the game when the king is trapped.

clue.text: One of twelve strange tales about a river

indicators.note: the rearranged word goes about, around, the river
strange signals the letters of the word after it are put in an odd order

parts.note: the Po is Italy's longest river

explanation.surface: Odd stories told about a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges TALES to ASTLE, and 'about' wraps the A and STLE around PO.
explanation.definitionFit: Jesus chose twelve disciples, each called by this title.

clue.text: Some hesitation in cutting out training

indicators.note: one piece sits in another

parts.note: excising means cutting out
er is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A pause in removing something during a training session.
explanation.definitionFit: Physical training or drilling is a form of working out, keeping fit by practice.

clue.text: Prevailed upon to accept rejected fragment brought in

indicators.note: one word taking in another, as a host accepts a guest, puts the second inside

parts.note: to induce someone is to persuade or prevail upon them

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so this word is read backwards

parts.note: an ort is a scrap or fragment of food

explanation.surface: Someone persuaded to take back a discarded scrap brings it indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns ORT into TRO, which 'to accept' places inside INDUCED. ORT, a leftover morsel, is a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: To introduce something is to bring it in, as a bill is brought into parliament.

clue.text: Part with money, say

indicators.note: 'say' signals that the word is spoken, and a word sounding like it is entered

parts.note: a sum is an amount of money

explanation.surface: Handing over cash, as it were.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part with money' reads as paying out, but 'Part' alone is the definition and 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Some of a thing is a portion of it, not the whole.

clue.text: Charges made by fruit people in Tim's new order

indicators.note: the fruit and people sit in the rearranged name
putting the letters of the name in a new order rearranges them

parts.note: a peach is a fruit
men are people

explanation.surface: Accusations levelled by fruit growers when Tim reorganises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new order' turns TIMS into IM and TS around PEACH and MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal accusations of misconduct against public officials are charges brought by a legislature.

clue.text: Doctor relative has a stop order

parts.note: Doctor Who is the TV time traveller, and 'who' is a relative pronoun

explanation.surface: A physician's family member issues a command to halt.
explanation.walkthrough: WHO works two ways: it completes Doctor Who, the long-running BBC science-fiction series, and it is a relative pronoun in grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: The call is shouted to a horse to make it halt, an order to stop.

clue.text: Silly about scholar being concerned with dialect

indicators.note: the word for silly goes about, around, the scholar's letters

parts.note: idiotic means silly or foolish
an MA, Master of Arts, is a scholar

explanation.surface: A daft academic studying regional speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Speech that is natural to a particular language or region, with its peculiar expressions, is idiomatic.

clue.text: Issue notes about the affair, having only superficial knowledge

indicators.note: the word for issuing notes wraps about the affair

parts.note: to issue musical notes is to sing
an affair in the sense of a business or concern is a matter

explanation.surface: Someone who airs notes on a scandal has only shallow learning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue notes' looks like printing money, but it is singing.
explanation.definitionFit: A slight, shallow acquaintance with a subject is a smattering of it.

clue.text: Cure film producer, possibly, being compassionate

indicators.note: a film producer may rework the material, so the letters of the words before are rearranged

explanation.surface: A movie maker might find a cure through being kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'producer, possibly' suggests a film producer, but it signals that CURE FILM is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A merciful person shows pity and forgiveness, which is compassion.

clue.text: Numbers still aboard, apparently

indicators.note: on board a ship means inside the steamship letters

parts.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship, the vessel implied
even can mean still, as in 'even more'

explanation.surface: Figures that are still on the ship, it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: Sevens are numbers, the figure 7 in plural, as in rugby sevens.

clue.text: French working girl gets tire replaced

indicators.note: the letters are put back in a new place, so rearranged

explanation.surface: A Parisian worker has a tyre changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replaced' reads like fitting a new tyre, but it rearranges GETS TIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: In France a grisette was a young working-class woman, often a seamstress or shop assistant.

clue.text: Television head taking off a recording

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: taking off someone is mimicking them, aping

explanation.surface: A TV boss departs from a recording session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking off' looks like departure, but it means imitating.
explanation.definitionFit: A taping is a recording, especially one made on magnetic tape.

clue.text: About mid-March, powerful sign

indicators.note: the word for powerful goes about the letter taken from the month

parts.note: potent means powerful

indicators.note: the middle of the month's name is wanted

explanation.surface: Around the middle of March comes a mighty omen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mid-March' looks like a date, but it is the central R of MARCH.
explanation.definitionFit: A portent is an omen or warning sign of what is to come.

clue.text: You must get this bit, for I can't anyway

indicators.note: anyway, meaning in any manner, tells the solver to arrange these letters however they will go

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs off a task they cannot manage and passes it on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' signals rearranging the letters of FOR I CANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A small part of a whole is a fraction of it.

clue.text: Minor key composition of princess

parts.note: a minor, legally, is an infant
A is a musical key

explanation.surface: A short piece in a minor key written by a princess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minor key' looks like music, but minor is a child and key gives A.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish or Portuguese king's daughter bears this title.

clue.text: Perhaps a local car

explanation.surface: A family car parked near the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is a British pub; the saloon bar is one of its rooms, and a saloon is also a sedan car.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub's lounge bar is one example of a drinking room; a sedan with an enclosed body is the car sense.

clue.text: Half-castes regret backing eastern people

indicators.note: going backwards, so the word for regret is reversed

parts.note: to rue is to regret
Asians are people from the East

explanation.surface: People of mixed parentage regret supporting Easterners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' looks like supporting, but it reverses RUE to give EUR. The definition is a dated, offensive term from the clue's era.
explanation.definitionFit: People of mixed European and Asian descent were once termed so, an old usage for those of mixed heritage.

clue.text: Cold comfort for a bungler

explanation.surface: Little consolation for someone who fouls things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold comfort' looks like an idiom for poor consolation, but here it is a warm tube for the hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A fur tube warms the hands in cold weather; to fumble a catch is to make a hash of it, and a clumsy person is called one.

clue.text: Nail seen on railway hoarding?

parts.note: BR stands for British Rail, the old national railway
a hoarding is a billboard bearing an ad

explanation.surface: A nail spotted on a railway billboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hoarding' looks like stockpiling, but it is a British billboard carrying advertisements.
explanation.definitionFit: A brad is a thin, small-headed wire tack used by carpenters.

clue.text: Thought the bride always carries it?

indicators.note: carries means holds inside, so the letters sit within the words that follow 'the'

explanation.surface: Something a bride constantly keeps with her.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea is a thought or notion formed in the mind.

clue.text: Square — right description of Clementine's father

parts.note: forty-nine is a square number, seven times seven

explanation.surface: A square and right-angled account of a girl's dad.
explanation.walkthrough: In the American folk song 'Oh My Darling, Clementine', her father was 'a miner, forty-niner', a prospector of the 1849 California gold rush.
explanation.definitionFit: The song names her father as a prospector who joined the 1849 gold rush.

clue.text: Entrance all who see game?

explanation.surface: A way into a stadium for every spectator.
explanation.definitionFit: A gateway is an entrance; the attendance, the crowd at a sporting match, is also so called.

clue.text: See Dr. Dunn's tea-blender

indicators.note: a blender mixes things, so the letters are mixed together

explanation.surface: Go and visit Dr Dunn, who blends tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text had 'Set' for 'See'. 'tea-blender' reads as a trade, but 'blender' shuffles DR DUNNS TEA.
explanation.definitionFit: To see a point is to grasp or comprehend it.
